subject: Science & Technology
question: Leo's computer is installing an update. He sees a bar filling up and knows he has about two minutes left. Before the 1980s, people often could not see this. Why does seeing the bar matter most for how people feel while waiting?

options.A: It makes the computer work faster
options.B: It reduces uncertainty so people wait more patiently
options.C: It makes the task take less time
options.D: It turns off the computer when done

explanation: The progress bar does not change how long the task takes, but it reduces uncertainty—so people feel less impatient. That is why designers added it: progress vs illusion of progress.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Jin's mom says 'your room won't clean itself.' Scientists say something similar about closed systems: left alone, they tend to become more messy, not neater. Why does this idea challenge the belief that 'the world just gets better over time'?

options.A: Because the world is not a closed system
options.B: Because progress is not automatic—we have to work for it
options.C: Because rooms are not part of nature

explanation: The Second Law (entropy) says things tend toward disorder. So 'progress' is not automatic; it takes effort. That is the heart of 'Progress, Not Regress.'

subject: Science & Technology
question: Jamie presses the 'close door' button in an elevator several times. The doors close a few seconds later. Later, Jamie learns the button does not actually control the doors. What ethical question does this raise?

options.B: Whether it is okay to give people a feeling of control when they have none—so they feel better while waiting
options.D: Whether Jamie should take the stairs

explanation: Placebo buttons make people feel in control but do not change the outcome. The theme: when is it okay to mislead people so they feel better about waiting? False signals.

subject: Science & Technology
question: An airport moved plane parking farther from the terminal so passengers had to walk longer to baggage claim. Total wait time was the same, but people complained less. What is the best explanation?

options.B: People feel less impatient when they are moving toward a goal than when they are standing still—even if the total time is the same
options.D: They were too tired to complain

explanation: Moving feels like progress; idling feels like being stuck. This ties to 'Progress, Not Regress' and why progress indicators matter.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Scientists use the Doomsday Clock to show how close they think the world is to a very bad outcome (like nuclear war or climate disaster). A critic says: 'But we can never really know when we are "there."' How does the clock still help?

options.A: It tells the real time of day
options.B: It pushes people and leaders to ask 'are we there yet?' and to act before it is too late—even if the exact moment is uncertain
options.C: It proves the world will end soon
options.D: It makes people scared for no reason

explanation: The Doomsday Clock is a symbol: it makes 'are we there yet?' visible so we can change course. Endings vs open endings.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Years ago, many people said 3D TVs would soon be in every home. Today they are rare. The same happened with nuclear-powered cars and food pills. What do these examples show about 'are we there yet?' in technology?

options.B: That some technologies stay 'almost there' for a long time because they are harder or less useful than people thought

explanation: 3D TVs, food pills, and similar ideas keep being promised but never quite arrive. Progress vs illusion of progress; Next Year in Futurism.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Some people assume 'the world just gets better over time.' Historians say that idea may be relatively new. Which law of physics challenges it by saying that left to themselves, closed systems tend toward disorder, not order?
explanation: The Second Law (entropy) says progress is not automatic—we have to work for it. Progress vs illusion of progress; 'Progress, Not Regress.'

subject: Science & Technology
question: In 2019, Google claimed 'quantum supremacy'—that its quantum computer had done something a classical computer could not do in reasonable time. Critics say that still does not mean we are 'there yet.' Why?

options.A: Because quantum computers are too expensive
options.B: Because quantum computers can run some tasks faster but still have almost no practical use in the real world—so 'are we there yet?' for everyday use is no

explanation: Quantum computers can beat classical ones on narrow tasks but lack widespread practical applications. Progress vs illusion of progress.

subject: Science & Technology
question: During the Cold War, the US and USSR raced to drill the deepest hole into the Earth's crust. The Soviet Kola Superdeep Borehole reached about 12,000 meters before the project ended. What does this story suggest about 'are we there yet?' for big projects?

options.A: That the US won the race
options.B: That even when we push a frontier (how deep we can go), projects can stop before we reach the goal—and we must choose what the next 'there' is
options.D: That Russia is better at science

explanation: The Kola Borehole shows megaproject delays and the question of what frontier to reach next. Next Year in Futurism.

subject: History
question: Captain Scott's team walked for months across ice to reach the South Pole. They often could not see how far was left. Why might that have made 'are we there yet?' harder for them?

options.B: Without clear progress indicators (knowing how much is left), waiting feels longer and more frustrating

explanation: Long journeys without progress indicators make 'are we there yet?' harder. Theme: waiting vs impatience; progress indicators.

subject: History
question: For years, the world had asked 'are we there yet?' about space. In 1969, millions watched on TV as a person first stepped on the Moon. Why did that moment answer the question for so many people?

options.B: It was a defined 'we got there'—humans had reached another world for the first time

explanation: Apollo 11 was a clear 'there' that the world had been working toward. Journey vs destination; endings vs open endings.

subject: History
question: Magellan's expedition (1519–1522) sailed from Europe around the world. The crew did not know exactly when they would get back. What does this show about 'are we there yet?' on such a journey?

options.B: When the goal is far and the end is uncertain, 'are we there yet?' can be asked for years

explanation: Circumnavigation took years with no clear ETA. Theme: waiting vs impatience; journey vs destination.

subject: History
question: Scott's Terra Nova Expedition aimed for the South Pole and crossed frozen land for years. Amundsen reached the Pole first; Scott's team got there later and did not survive the return. What does this show about 'are we there yet?' for such expeditions?

options.B: Reaching 'there' (the Pole) was not enough—getting back safely was part of the journey, and they did not make it

explanation: 'There' can include the return. Journey vs destination; megaproject delays; endings vs open endings.

subject: History
question: Traders on the Silk Road traveled from China to the Mediterranean. The full trip could take a year or more. Why might traders have used milestones (e.g. certain cities) to know where they were?

options.B: Milestones answer 'are we there yet?' by showing how far you have come and how much is left

explanation: Milestones (cities, landmarks) work as progress indicators on long journeys. Measuring progress; journey vs destination.

subject: History
question: Columbus set out to reach Asia by sailing west. He did not find Asia but found new lands. How does his journey relate to 'are we there yet?'?

options.B: He was looking for one 'there' (Asia) but reached a different 'there' (the Americas)—so the goal and the destination can change along the way

explanation: The intended 'there' and the actual 'there' can differ. Journey vs destination; progress vs illusion of progress.

subject: History
question: Scott's Terra Nova Expedition to the Antarctic is sometimes seen as heroic and sometimes as a warning about overconfidence. Why might both views focus on the same journey?

options.B: The same journey can be read as 'we kept going' or as 'we were not ready for the return'—so 'are we there yet?' includes whether we prepared for the full journey

explanation: Defining 'there' (Pole only vs. Pole and back) changes how we judge the journey. Journey vs destination; endings vs open endings.

subject: History
question: The 'end of history' thesis suggested that liberal democracy might be the final form of government. A critic says: 'But history did not stop.' What are they disagreeing about?

options.B: Whether we have 'arrived' at a final destination or whether 'are we there yet?' has no permanent answer

explanation: Fukuyama's thesis asked if we had reached the 'end' of political progress. Theme: endings vs open endings; progress vs illusion.

subject: History
question: The Space Race asked which nation would first put a human on the Moon. When the first landing happened in 1969, why did many people treat it as the answer to 'are we there yet?' for space?

options.B: It was the defined goal both sides had set—so reaching it was a clear 'we got there' moment

explanation: The Moon was the shared 'there.' Reaching it answered the question for the world. Journey vs destination; measuring progress.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In an ancient Greek story, a hero spends years trying to get home and faces many obstacles. The question 'are we there yet?' is at the heart of the tale. What is this story called?
explanation: The Odyssey is the story of Odysseus's long journey home. Theme: journey vs destination; waiting vs impatience.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In the Odyssey, the god Poseidon is angry at Odysseus and causes storms and delays. Why does this make 'are we there yet?' central to the story?

options.B: Obstacles and delays keep the hero from 'getting there'—so the question of when (or if) he will arrive drives the plot

explanation: Delays and obstacles make the journey long and uncertain. Theme: waiting vs impatience; journey vs destination.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In 'The Hobbit,' Bilbo's adventure is described as 'There and Back Again.' What does this title suggest about the story?

options.B: The journey has a 'there' (the goal) and a return—so 'are we there yet?' is asked twice: going and coming back

explanation: 'There and Back Again' frames the story as a round trip with a defined 'there.' Journey vs destination.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In the Odyssey, Poseidon delays Odysseus's return home. Why might an author include a character or force that keeps the hero from 'getting there'?

options.B: To stretch the journey and keep the audience asking 'are we there yet?'
options.C: To show that gods are kind

explanation: Delays create tension and keep 'are we there yet?' central. Theme: waiting vs impatience; journey vs destination.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In Dante's Divine Comedy, the narrator travels through Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. What does this structure suggest about 'are we there yet?' in the poem?

options.B: 'There' is reached in stages—each part is a step toward the final destination (heaven)

explanation: The three parts are milestones on one long journey. Theme: journey vs destination; progress indicators.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In 'The Pilgrim's Progress,' the hero travels toward the Celestial City. The story is an allegory. What does the journey stand for?

options.B: The path of life and the question of whether we ever 'arrive' at salvation or fulfillment

explanation: The pilgrim's journey is a metaphor for life and the search for a 'there' (salvation). Theme: journey vs destination; endings vs open endings.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In 'Waiting for Godot,' two characters wait for someone who never clearly arrives. Why might this play be read as a comment on 'are we there yet?'?

options.B: It asks whether we ever really 'get there' or whether we are always waiting—so the question has no clear answer

explanation: The play explores endless waiting and the possibility that 'there' never comes. Theme: endings vs open endings; waiting vs impatience.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In the Odyssey, the hero's long return home (nostos) is often read as more than a trip. What deeper question does it raise?

options.B: Whether we ever find where we belong—so 'are we there yet?' becomes 'have we found our place?'

explanation: Nostos is linked to identity and belonging. Theme: journey vs destination; endings vs open endings.

subject: Art & Music
question: Early 20th-century artists painted cars and trains moving fast. They wanted to show speed and the feeling of 'are we there yet?' in a single moment. Which movement was this?
explanation: Futurism focused on speed, machines, and movement through time. Theme: journey vs destination; progress vs illusion.

subject: Art & Music
question: A symphony has several movements and can last a long time. When you listen, you might wonder when it will end. Why might a composer structure a piece in clear movements?

options.B: To give the listener a sense of progress—each movement is a step toward the end, so 'are we there yet?' has answers along the way

explanation: Movements work like progress indicators in a long piece. Theme: progress indicators; journey vs destination.

subject: Art & Music
question: Which early 20th-century art movement tried to show motion and the question of 'when' we are in time—like capturing 'are we there yet?' in a single image?
explanation: Futurism dealt with speed, technology, and representing time and motion. Theme: journey vs destination; progress vs illusion.

subject: Art & Music
question: In music, a refrain or leitmotif is a theme that comes back again and again. Why might that create a feeling of 'are we there yet?' for the listener?

options.B: It gives a sense of 'we're back there again'—a return to a familiar place, so the listener knows where they are in the journey

explanation: Recurring themes mark progress and return. Theme: journey vs destination; progress indicators.

subject: Art & Music
question: Holst's 'The Planets' has one movement per planet, like stops on a trip. What does this structure do for the listener?

options.B: It gives a sense of progress—each movement is a 'there' (a planet) on the way through the piece

explanation: Each movement is a milestone in the musical journey. Theme: journey vs destination; progress indicators.

subject: Art & Music
question: Which early 20th-century movement made speed, technology, and the representation of time and motion central to art?
explanation: Futurism focused on velocity, progress, and representing 'when' we are. Theme: journey vs destination; progress vs illusion.

subject: Art & Music
question: Wagner's Ring cycle is four operas that tell one long story. Leitmotifs (recurring themes) bring back characters and ideas. Why might that create a sense of 'are we there yet?' for the audience?

options.B: Recurring themes mark where we are in the story—we 'return' to familiar moments, so we know how far we have come

explanation: Leitmotifs work as progress markers in a long narrative. Theme: journey vs destination; progress indicators.

subject: Social Studies
question: The Human Development Index (HDI) uses health, education, and living standards to see how well a country is doing. A critic says: 'But that doesn't tell us if people feel they have gotten there.' What is the critic asking?

options.B: Whether the way we measure 'are we there yet?' for a country really captures what matters to people

explanation: HDI is one way to ask 'are we there yet?' for development; the critic asks if it reflects what people value. Theme: measuring progress.

subject: Social Studies
question: When sailors cross the Equator (the line around the middle of the Earth), they sometimes celebrate. Why might they treat crossing it as a special moment?

options.A: The Equator is the hottest place
options.B: It is a milestone—a clear 'we got there' (to the middle of the world) that breaks up the long journey
options.D: They have nothing else to do

explanation: Crossing the Equator is a progress milestone. Theme: journey vs destination; progress indicators.

subject: Social Studies
question: The HDI measures health, education, and standard of living. Why might a country care about such a measure for 'are we there yet?' in development?

options.B: To have a shared way to see how far the country has come and how much is left to do

explanation: HDI answers 'how far have we come?' for development. Theme: measuring progress; journey vs destination.

subject: Social Studies
question: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) set targets for 2030. Why might having a date like 2030 matter for 'are we there yet?' in global development?

options.B: It defines when 'there' is—so we can ask 'are we there yet?' and check progress toward that moment

explanation: A target date defines 'there' and allows progress checks. Theme: measuring progress; journey vs destination.

subject: Social Studies
question: Some scholars say 'development' should not be seen as one linear journey to a single 'there.' Which view stresses many possible paths and local context?
explanation: Post-development questions a single 'there' and stresses diverse paths. Theme: journey vs destination; progress vs illusion.

subject: Social Studies
question: Amartya Sen's capability approach asks whether people have the freedom to achieve what they value. How does this change the question 'are we there yet?' for development?

options.A: It makes it only about money
options.B: 'There' becomes not just income but whether people can lead the lives they value—a broader idea of progress
options.C: It only applies to rich countries

explanation: Capabilities broaden what 'there' means. Theme: measuring progress; journey vs destination.

subject: Special Area
question: When people get closer to a goal, they often try harder. Psychologists call this the goal gradient effect. Why might that relate to 'are we there yet?'?

options.B: When we feel we are 'almost there,' we speed up—so the sense of 'how much is left' affects our effort

explanation: Feeling 'almost there' changes behavior. Theme: progress indicators; journey vs destination.

subject: Special Area
question: When we have to wait for something we want, we often feel impatient. What makes impatience stronger in many situations?

options.B: Not knowing how long is left (uncertainty) often makes waiting feel longer and more frustrating

explanation: Uncertainty increases impatience. Theme: waiting vs impatience; progress indicators.

subject: Special Area
question: The goal gradient effect says we often speed up as we get closer to a goal. How does this relate to 'are we there yet?'?

options.B: Our sense of 'how much is left' (are we there yet?) affects how hard we try—closer feels more motivating
options.D: It only applies to physical distance

explanation: Progress perception affects motivation. Theme: progress indicators; journey vs destination.

subject: Special Area
question: Some philosophers say the journey can matter more than the destination. What might they say about the question 'are we there yet?'?

options.A: It is the only question that matters
options.B: They might say that focusing only on 'there' can make us miss the value of the process—so the question might be the wrong one

explanation: Stoicism and process philosophy value the process. Theme: journey vs destination; waiting vs impatience.

subject: Special Area
question: In project management, the moment when everyone agrees the project is complete is called closure or sign-off. Why might that moment matter for 'are we there yet?'?

options.B: It is the formal moment when 'are we there yet?' becomes yes—the project has 'arrived'

explanation: Closure defines the end of the project. Theme: journey vs destination; progress indicators.

subject: Special Area
question: Zeno's paradox says a runner must cover half the remaining distance, then half of that, and so on—so they never reach the finish line. What does this raise about 'are we there yet?'?

options.B: A philosophical question about whether we can ever truly 'get there' in a strict sense (infinite divisibility)

explanation: Zeno challenges whether we can ever 'arrive' in a strict sense. Theme: journey vs destination; endings vs open endings.

subject: Special Area
question: The hedonic treadmill says that after we reach a goal, we often return to a baseline level of happiness. What does this suggest about 'are we there yet?'?

options.B: That 'there' may keep moving—when we get there, we may soon want the next 'there,' so the question may have no final answer
options.D: That it only applies to travel

explanation: Satisfaction can be temporary; 'there' can be a moving target. Theme: journey vs destination; progress vs illusion.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In the fable of the tortoise and the hare, the tortoise wins by moving steadily. What does this suggest about 'are we there yet?' and finishing?

options.B: Steady progress can get you 'there' even when others are faster but don't keep going

explanation: The fable links steady progress to reaching the goal. Theme: journey vs destination; progress vs illusion.

subject: History
question: Families on the Oregon Trail traveled by wagon for months. They could not know exactly when they would arrive. Why might that have made 'are we there yet?' a daily question for children?

options.B: When the journey is long and the end is uncertain, people keep asking how much is left

explanation: Long, uncertain journeys make 'are we there yet?' constant. Theme: waiting vs impatience; journey vs destination.

subject: Art & Music
question: A pilgrimage is a long journey to a place that is important for someone's religion or beliefs. Why might pilgrims ask 'are we there yet?' on the way?

options.B: The journey is long and the destination is a defined 'there' they are working toward

explanation: Pilgrimages have a clear 'there' and a long journey. Theme: journey vs destination; progress indicators.

subject: Science & Technology
question: In the 1770s, a 'chess-playing machine' called the Mechanical Turk beat many players. Famous people like Benjamin Franklin played it. It was later revealed that a person was hidden inside. What does this story teach us about technology that seems 'there' but is not yet?

options.B: That sometimes what looks like 'we are there' (a machine that thinks) is actually a human doing the work—and that we still use this idea today to test products before building the real thing
options.C: That Benjamin Franklin was easily fooled

explanation: The Mechanical Turk was a prototype-vs-deception example. Wizard of Oz testing still fakes the tech to see how people react before building it.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Sana is filling out a long form on a website. A bar at the top shows she is 60% done. She decides to finish instead of leaving. What is the main reason progress bars in apps often lead to more people finishing?

options.B: They give a sense of how far along you are, so you feel closer to the end

explanation: Progress bars do not change the task, but they show 'how much is left'—so people feel they are getting somewhere and are more likely to finish.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Sam has three homework tasks. He finishes two and keeps thinking about the one he did not finish, even during dinner. Why do unfinished tasks often stick in our minds more than finished ones?

options.B: Because our brain tends to hold on to incomplete things until we feel we have closed the loop
options.C: Because we forget finished tasks right away

explanation: Psychologists call this the Zeigarnik Effect: unfinished tasks create tension that stays until we complete them or decide to drop them—'are we there yet?' in our head.

subject: Science & Technology
question: A toy company makes a rough cardboard version of a new game and lets kids play with it before building the real box and pieces. Why is this step useful?

options.A: Because cardboard is cheaper than plastic
options.B: Because it lets the company see if the idea works and what to change before spending a lot on the final product
options.D: Because the real product is never finished

explanation: This is prototyping: testing an early version to answer 'are we there yet?' before committing to the final design. Drafts vs finished work.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Maya's game is loading. A bar moves back and forth but never shows how much is left. She is not sure whether to wait or close the app. How is this different from a progress bar that shows '50% done'?

options.B: The moving bar does not reduce uncertainty—she still does not know if she is almost there or have a long wait
options.C: The moving bar uses more battery
options.D: The moving bar is a different color

explanation: A bar that moves without showing 'how much left' gives the feeling something is happening but not real progress information—progress vs illusion of progress.

subject: Science & Technology
question: When the internet goes out, Google Chrome shows a small game you can play while waiting. Why would a company add a game to a 'waiting' screen instead of just showing 'Loading...'?

options.A: To make the internet come back faster
options.B: To give people something to do so waiting feels shorter and less frustrating
options.C: To teach people how to use Chrome

explanation: Filling wait time with an activity (like Chrome's Dinosaur Game or Ridge Racer's loading mini-game) makes the wait feel less long—waiting vs impatience.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Alex starts a puzzle, leaves it half done, and goes to play outside. Later, Alex keeps thinking about the puzzle more than about the game outside. What best explains why the unfinished puzzle sticks in Alex's mind?

options.A: Puzzles are more fun than playing outside
options.B: Unfinished tasks often create a kind of mental 'open loop' that stays until we finish or let go
options.C: Playing outside is bad for memory

explanation: The Zeigarnik Effect: incomplete tasks tend to stay in mind. It is why we ask 'are we there yet?'—we want to close the loop. Unfinished tasks psychology.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Scientists use a 'Doomsday Clock' to show how close they think the world is to a very bad event (like nuclear danger or climate crisis). What is the main purpose of such a clock?

options.A: To tell the real time of day
options.B: To warn people and leaders that we need to act before it is too late—to ask 'are we there yet?' in a serious way
options.C: To prove that the world will end soon
options.D: To make people scared for no reason

explanation: The Doomsday Clock is a symbol: it tries to show how close we are to catastrophe so we can change course. Endings vs open endings; measuring progress toward danger.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Sea turtles travel across the ocean and still find the beach where they were born. They do not use maps or phones. What is the best explanation science has for how they know where they are?

options.B: They can sense the Earth's magnetic field—like a built-in compass—so they know direction and position

explanation: Many animals use magnetoreception (sensing the magnetic field) to navigate. It is their way of answering 'are we there yet?' without maps. Journey vs destination.

subject: Science & Technology
question: People have said 'flying cars are just a few years away' for decades, but we still do not have them. The same is true for pills that replace a full meal. Why do some technologies stay 'almost there' for so long?

options.B: They are harder to build or less useful than people thought, so they never quite arrive

explanation: Flying cars and food pills keep being promised but face big technical or practical problems. Progress vs illusion of progress—'are we there yet?' for technology.

subject: Science & Technology
question: A team has an idea for a new water bottle. Instead of building thousands of bottles right away, they make a few by hand and give them to friends to try. What is the main advantage of this approach?

options.B: They can learn what works and what does not before spending a lot of time and money on the final product
options.D: It is faster than making thousands

explanation: Making a quick test version (rapid prototyping) answers 'are we there yet?' before full production. Prototypes vs final products.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Jordan asks a chatbot to write a small program instead of typing the code by hand. The program works, but a teacher says 'everyone getting there so easily might mean we get more programs that break or no one knows how to fix.' What is the teacher worried about?

options.B: That the chatbot is too slow
options.C: That making it easy to 'get there' might lead to more low-quality or unsupported software

explanation: Vibe coding (AI writing code) makes it easier to reach a result, but the worry is quality and who maintains it—progress vs illusion of progress.

subject: Science & Technology
question: In the 1770s, a machine that seemed to play chess amazed people around the world. It turned out a person was hidden inside, moving the pieces. Why might a company today still use a hidden person instead of a real robot when testing a new product?

options.B: To see how people react to the idea before building the real thing—fake it to test, then build

explanation: Wizard of Oz testing: fake the tech with a human to learn what users want before building the real product. Prototype vs deception; rehearsal and iteration.

subject: Science & Technology
question: A store said you could 'just walk out' and your card would be charged by AI—no cashier. Later people learned that at first, workers were watching video and writing down what people took. What ethical question does this raise?

options.B: Whether it is okay to say a system is 'AI' when humans are doing the work, and whether 'fake it till you make it' is fair if you eventually get there

explanation: The store presented progress (AI) while humans did the work, then later replaced them. Prototype vs deception; is it okay to mislead to get to the real thing?

subject: Science & Technology
question: Scientists say the part of the brain that helps with planning and 'thinking before you act' keeps growing into your twenties. Why might the theme 'Are We There Yet?' apply to being a teenager?

options.B: Because teenagers are not quite children and not quite adults—they are in between, 'not there yet' in one sense
options.D: Because the brain stops growing at 20

explanation: Adolescence is a liminal stage: not quite there yet as an adult. The theme 'Going Pains' asks whether there are advantages to being in-between.

subject: Science & Technology
question: A small beetle rolls a ball at night and still finds its way. Scientists found it can use the band of stars we call the Milky Way to know which way to go. What does this show about 'are we there yet?' for animals?

options.A: That beetles are smarter than humans
options.B: That some animals can tell where they are and where they are going without maps or phones—they have their own way of knowing
options.C: That the Milky Way is close to Earth

explanation: Dung beetles use the night sky to navigate. Animals have their own ways of answering 'are we there yet?'—journey vs destination; home and wandering.

subject: Science & Technology
question: When Kim opens an app, a picture or logo appears for a few seconds before the main screen loads. Why would designers show this instead of a blank white screen?

options.A: To make the app load faster
options.B: To give people something to look at so the wait feels shorter and the app feels more polished

explanation: A splash screen fills wait time and signals that something is loading—progress indicators and design; waiting vs impatience.

subject: Science & Technology
question: An app shows a progress bar while users fill out a long form. More people finish the form when the bar is there than when it is not. Some people ask: is it okay for designers to use this to 'push' people to finish? What is the main ethical question?

options.A: Whether progress bars are true or false
options.B: Whether it is okay to design interfaces that persuade people to do something—and where persuasion becomes manipulation

explanation: Progress bars nudge people to complete tasks. The theme asks: when does helping people finish cross the line into pushing them? Design and ethics.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Neil Armstrong (the first person on the Moon) said we predict too much for the next year and too little for the next ten. What does this suggest about why some technologies seem 'almost here' for a long time?

options.A: That we should not build new technology
options.B: That scientists are bad at planning
options.C: That it is hard to know exactly when a technology will really arrive—we often get the short-term wrong
options.D: That the Moon is far away

explanation: Science is not good at predicting exactly when things will happen. That is why 'flying cars in five years' keeps repeating—progress vs illusion of progress.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Nikola Tesla built a big tower and said it would soon send wireless messages around the world. The project ran out of money and was never finished. What does this story show about 'are we there yet?' in technology?

options.B: That some projects that promise 'we are almost there' never get there—they run out of time, money, or support
options.C: That Tesla was a bad inventor

explanation: Wardenclyffe is an example of a promised technology that never arrived. Megaproject delays; progress vs illusion of progress.

subject: Science & Technology
question: Scientists studying a lake notice that the amount of green stuff in the water (algae) suddenly goes up and down a lot—more than before. They say this can be a warning sign. What might they be worried about?

explanation: Each episode is a step—and the finale (or next episode) is the 'there' we are waiting for. Theme: measuring progress.

subject: Literature & Media
question: After a long trip or adventure, the hero sets off to go home. That journey back has its own dangers and its own 'are we there yet?' What do we call the journey home after a long trip?
explanation: Going home is a different journey with its own 'there'—so the question starts again when the hero sets off back. Theme: journey vs destination.

subject: Literature & Media
question: A story about a tortoise and a hare teaches that steady progress can get you 'there' even when others are faster but don't keep going. What kind of story teaches a lesson, often with animals as characters?
explanation: The fable links steady progress to reaching the goal. Theme: journey vs destination; progress vs illusion.

subject: Literature & Media
question: The reader follows a story from the first page to the last. The person who decided where the story starts and ends defines 'there' for the reader. Who is that person?
explanation: The author chooses the goal and the path—so they define when the story has 'gotten there.' Theme: journey vs destination.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In a long book, each section is like a step toward the end. The reader can see how far they have come. What do we call one such section of a long book?
explanation: Chapters are milestones—they show how far you have come and how much is left. Theme: measuring progress.

subject: Literature & Media
question: A story is brief but still has a beginning and an end. The reader still follows from start to end and waits for the conclusion. What kind of story is this?
explanation: Even a short story has a journey—we follow from start to end and wait for the conclusion. Theme: journey vs destination.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In a story, characters say things like 'How much longer?' or 'When will we arrive?' When characters ask the question, they make it central to the story. What do we call the words that characters say to each other?
explanation: Dialogue can make 'are we there yet?' explicit—so the audience asks it too. Theme: waiting vs impatience.

subject: Literature & Media
question: A story keeps us guessing who did it or what happened until the very end. The moment when we find out feels like 'we got there.' What kind of story often makes that moment the 'there'?
explanation: The reveal is the 'there'—the moment when the story's main question is finally answered. Theme: journey vs destination.

subject: Literature & Media
question: A story is set on a long journey through space or time. The characters keep asking when they will arrive. What kind of story often puts 'are we there yet?' at the center?
explanation: Long journeys (to another planet, another time) have a clear goal but an uncertain or long path—so the question is central. Theme: journey vs destination.

subject: Literature & Media
question: A hero goes on a quest—to find a ring, save a kingdom, or reach a distant land. The path is long and dangerous, and we keep asking when they will get there. What kind of story often drives 'are we there yet?' with such quests?
explanation: A quest has a defined 'there' but a long, dangerous path—so we keep asking when they will get there. Theme: journey vs destination.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In a long book, each section has a name that acts like a sign on the journey—showing where we are and how much is left. What do we call the name of such a section?
explanation: Chapter titles are like signs on a journey—they show where we are and how much is left. Theme: measuring progress.

subject: Literature & Media
question: Some stories teach that focusing only on 'there' can make us miss the value of the way. So 'are we there yet?' might not be the only question. What idea does this express?

options.B: The journey can be as important as the destination

explanation: Theme can question whether 'there' is all that matters. Journey vs destination; waiting vs impatience.

subject: Literature & Media
question: Samuel Beckett's 'Waiting for Godot' is often read as a story about endless waiting and the question of whether we ever 'arrive.' Which theatrical tradition is it most associated with?
explanation: Waiting for Godot is a key work of the Theatre of the Absurd. It explores whether we ever 'get there' and what meaning exists in the wait.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus takes a very long journey home. Which god is mainly responsible for delaying his return?
explanation: Poseidon is angry at Odysseus (who hurt his son Polyphemus) and causes storms and obstacles, so the question 'Are we there yet?' is central to the story.

subject: Literature & Media
question: In Dante's Divine Comedy, the journey through the afterlife is structured in three parts. What are they?
explanation: Dante travels through Inferno (Hell), Purgatorio (Purgatory), and Paradiso (Heaven). The poem is one long 'are we there yet?' toward divine arrival.

subject: Literature & Media
question: John Bunyan's 'The Pilgrim's Progress' describes a journey that symbolizes what?
